newsitem.title: UK: POLL-UK exporters narrowly oppose single currency.
newsitem.headline: POLL-UK exporters narrowly oppose single currency.

text.p: British exporters oppose the introduction of a European single currency, but only by a fine margin, a survey revealed on Wednesday.

The poll, conducted by international credit insurer NCM and the UK Institute of Export, found that 47 percent voted 'No' to European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), compared with 48 percent in 1996.

Forty four percent of the 850 companies who replied to the survey said they wanted a single currency, compared with a previous 43 percent. The number of undecided was nine percent, unchanged from last year.
Despite 44 percent of the respondents showing approval of EMU and its scheduled start in 1999 only 11 percent of companies were preparing for its introduction, the survey said.

When the responding companies were broken down by size it was evident that the greatest opposition to EMU came from smaller firms, with turnovers of up to a million pounds and larger ones turning over between 25-50 million pounds.

In both brackets, 55 percent of respondents voted against EMU. The biggest supporters of EMU came in the 50 million or more turnover sector, where 60 percent voted in favour of the single currency and 40 against.
Scotland proved to be the most EMU-friendly part of Britain, registering a 58 percent 'yes' vote, unchanged from last year, and 42 percent against EMU, up from 37 percent in 1996.

Wales was well above the UK average for dissent of the single currency, with 75 percent voting against the single currency, up from 19 percent last year, and 25 percent showing approval compared to the previous 81.
The respondents, ranging from multi-nationals to owner-managers, also voiced their opposition to introduction of the Social Chapter in the UK.
The poll showed 69 percent were against the European social chapter, 21 percent were in favour, and 10 percent were undecided.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair has accepted the social chapter, a European Union protocol, which guarantees minimum employment rights, such as parental leave and employer consultation.
